sections.h2: Who pays the realty transfer fee
sections.html:
The seller pays it. The Realty Transfer Fee (RTF) is a state charge that the seller owes when a deed is recorded, and the supplemental percent fee lands on the seller too. Any conveyance of title to New Jersey real property is covered unless the deed or the transfer matches a listed exemption.

The amount is figured on the consideration written in the deed. In some cases the Division of Taxation instead takes the assessed value of the property and divides it by the Director's Ratio for the municipality. That ratio comes from the certification of the Table of Equalized Valuations, and filers use the prior year's certification for a deed dated in a given year.

Anyone claiming a full or partial exemption must file Form RTF-1, the Affidavit of Consideration for Use by Seller, with the deed. For a sheriff's sale, the applicant also files Form RTF-8, which lists other mortgagees and liens. RTF-8 is not an exemption.

Brackets of $500 drive the math, and the price decides which ladder you climb. Totals of $350,000 or less use the lower ladder below.

Standard seller rates when total consideration is $350,000 or less
Consideration bracketRate per $500
$0 to $150,000$2.00
$150,000 to $200,000$3.35
$200,000 to $350,000$3.90

Once the total passes $350,000, a higher ladder applies. Its first slice, up to $150,000, runs $2.90 for each $500. The slice up to $200,000 runs $4.25 and the slice up to $550,000 runs $4.80. Beyond that you pay $5.30 up to $850,000, then $5.80 up to $1,000,000, then $6.05 on whatever remains.

The exact figure shows up on your settlement statement.

sections.h2: The extra percent fee on sales over $1 million
sections.html:
The Graduated Percent Fee, often called the mansion tax, applies when the consideration is more than $1,000,000. It is charged on the total price, and the percentage climbs with the bracket. The seller is statutorily responsible for it along with the RTF.

The percentage steps up with the price. A price over $1 million and up to $2 million draws 1 percent. Over $2 million and up to $2.5 million it is 2 percent, and over $2.5 million and up to $3 million it is 2.5 percent. Above $3 million and up to $3.5 million the fee is 3 percent, and anything over $3.5 million pays 3.5 percent.

The fee covers deeds for Class 2 residential property, Class 3A farms that contain a building suited for residential use, Class 4A commercial property other than industrial or apartment, and Class 4C cooperative units. Exemptions are claimed on Form RTF-1EE, which goes with every deed over $1 million and every commercial transfer.

Some deeds owe no RTF at all. The exemptions are read narrowly, so a transfer missing from the list pays the fee even when the reason behind it seems sympathetic. Exempt deeds include:

  • any deed with consideration under $100
  • a deed between husband and wife, or between parent and child
  • an executor's or administrator's deed to a devisee or heir that distributes the estate under the will or the intestacy laws
  • a deed filed within three months after a divorce decree ends the marriage of grantor and grantee
  • a deed that gives or releases security for a debt, or that confirms or corrects a deed already recorded
  • deeds on partition, on a sale for delinquent taxes, or from a receiver, bankruptcy trustee or assignee for creditors

Family cases produce most of the questions. A sale from parents to their daughter and son-in-law is exempt as parent to child. A father selling to his daughter and her live-in boyfriend gets an exemption on half of the price, and the other half is taxed. A legally adopted child counts as a child, but a stepchild does not unless the stepparent adopted him or her.

An executor who sells to an heir named in the will, or an heir under the intestacy rules, is exempt. A sale to anyone else is not. If a will tells the executor to sell and divide the money, the bequest is treated as a gift of money, so that sale pays the fee. Placing a house in trust for children is also taxable because the grantor gives up the benefits of ownership.

A divorce settlement that is simply folded into a judgment does not qualify as specific performance of a final judgment. The deed has to follow the decree closely, within the 90-day window, to use the divorce exemption. Attorney-prepared deeds in quitclaim form that move a freehold interest are treated as taxable transfers.

sections.h2: Reduced rates for seniors and disabled sellers
sections.html:
Lower partial rates are open to sellers who are 62 or older, to blind or disabled sellers, and to low and moderate income housing transfers. On a total of $350,000 or less, the reduced rate is $0.50 per $500 through $150,000, then $1.25 per $500 between $150,000 and $350,000.

On a total above $350,000, the reduced rates start at $1.40 per $500 for the first $150,000 and climb to $3.40 per $500 above $1,000,000. You claim the rate on a notarized Form RTF-1 recorded with the deed.

The rate belongs to the seller personally. An estate, a trust or a company cannot use it, and a senior who moves a house into a trust gives it up. On a farm sale, only the share of the price tied to the residence and the land needed to enjoy it qualifies, usually the Class 3A portion.

sections.h2: Where the fee is paid, and what if the county is wrong
sections.html:
Payment goes to the county recording officer at the counter. The land's own county is the only valid place to file. A deed that lands in a different county must be filed again in the right one, with a State refund request on Form RTF-3, and the county portion has to be reclaimed from the wrong county's recording office.

Ask the county clerk for the current recording charges, because those are county fees and sit on top of the state fee. Find the RTF line on the seller's closing statement and ask whoever runs your closing how it will reach the recording officer.

A few steps keep the fee from surprising you at the table.

  • Settle early whether an exemption or reduced rate fits, and tell the closing agent so a notarized Form RTF-1 goes to the recording office with the deed.
  • On a price above $1,000,000, expect Form RTF-1EE to travel with the deed.
  • Confirm the county where the property sits, because recording happens there.
  • Find the RTF line on the seller's closing statement and check that the bracket matches the price.

The fee comes out of the seller's proceeds at closing. A cash buyer does not change who owes it, but a quicker closing means the fee is settled sooner.

faqs.q: Is the realty transfer fee paid by the buyer or the seller?
faqs.a: The seller pays it. The RTF is imposed on the seller for recording the deed, and the Graduated Percent Fee falls on the seller too.

faqs.q: Does the fee change with the sale price?
faqs.a: Yes. It is charged per $500 of consideration in brackets, with one schedule for prices of $350,000 or less and a steeper one above that. Sales over $1,000,000 also carry the percent fee.

faqs.q: Is a sale between a parent and a child exempt?
faqs.a: Yes, a deed between parent and child is exempt, and that includes a legally adopted child. A stepchild relationship does not qualify unless the stepparent adopted the child.

faqs.q: Does the senior citizen rate work if my house is in a trust?
faqs.a: No. The reduced rate is a personal exemption and a trust cannot use it. A senior who deeds the house to a trust and later sells through it pays the standard rates.

faqs.q: What form do I file to claim an exemption?
faqs.a: File Form RTF-1, the Affidavit of Consideration for Use by Seller, with the deed. It must be notarized for a partial exemption. Deeds priced above $1,000,000 also carry Form RTF-1EE for the percent fee.
